proposal: The President should direct DOJ to bring criminal Federal Election Campaign Act cases only for clear violations, to take FEC enforcement actions, regulations and advisory opinions into account, and not to prosecute under readings the FEC has rejected (including through tied votes), and to defend the FEC in litigation when commissioners cannot agree to authorize its defense. Congress could also be asked to remove the FEC's independent litigating authority, and the FEC or DOJ should publish guidance on FECA provisions struck down by courts.

status_summary: No presidential or DOJ directive limiting criminal FECA prosecutions to clear violations, no DOJ defense of the FEC when it cannot authorize its own, no bill to end the FEC's independent litigating authority, and no DOJ or FEC guidance on court-voided FECA provisions was found in records and systematic checks run through 2026-10-18. The FEC has lacked a quorum since 2025-05-01 (two commissioners remain, both Democrats) and told the D.C. district court on 2026-03-31 and 2026-04-24 that it cannot authorize a defense; the nominations of two Republican commissioners announced 2026-02-11 had no scheduled confirmation hearing as of August 2026. In Seegers v. FEC (D.D.C., No. 1:26-cv-00276), a suit to compel FEC action on an administrative complaint, the clerk entered default against the FEC on 2026-07-08; the plaintiff's motion (filed 2026-07-28) reports service on the U.S. Attorney for D.C. (2026-02-24) and the Attorney General (delivered 2026-03-04) and describes no DOJ appearance, which is the situation the chapter asks DOJ to prevent. Related DOJ and White House actions are of a different kind: a 2025-04-24 presidential memorandum directs the Attorney General to investigate straw-donor and foreign contributions made through online fundraising platforms, the Public Integrity Section had shrunk from about 30 prosecutors to fewer than five by May 2025 per press reports, and in NRSC v. FEC (decided 2026-06-30) the Solicitor General's office argued against FECA's party coordination limits, a position the chapter also takes (p. 866). None of these sets a standard for choosing FECA prosecutions or provides for DOJ to defend the FEC.

timeline.event: Executive order 'Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies' extends OIRA review of significant rules to independent agencies, amends the regulatory review order so that 'agency' includes the Federal Election Commission, and states that the President's and Attorney General's legal interpretations control for executive branch employees, including in litigation positions. Context only: it does not address FECA prosecution or FEC defense.

Presidential memorandum directs the Attorney General, with the Treasury Secretary, to use all lawful authority to investigate unlawful straw-donor and foreign contributions made through online fundraising platforms and to report within 180 days; it cites 52 U.S.C. 30121 and 30122 and does not mention the FEC. A press report of 2025-10-10 describes the probe as in its final days, with no grand jury, subpoenas or charges mentioned.

A press report (dated by its URL to 2025-05-17) says the Public Integrity Section, which handles election crimes including campaign finance offenses, had shrunk from about 30 prosecutors to fewer than five, and that DOJ was considering a Justice Manual change letting U.S. attorneys' offices charge members of Congress without the section's approval; DOJ said no final decisions had been made. AP had reported the planned reduction on 2025-03-11. Final staffing and the outcome of the proposal were not confirmed.

In Democratic National Committee v. Trump (D.D.C., No. 25-00587), Judge Ali dismisses for lack of jurisdiction a challenge to the application of the 2025-02-18 order to the FEC, because the committees alleged no concrete or imminent application; defendants told the court they knew of no attempt or plan to apply the order's legal-interpretation provision to the FEC, and the court left open a later challenge.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for D.C. (opinion posted by the FEC)

timeline.event: The President announces nominations of Ashley Stow (term to 2029) and Andrew Woodson (term to 2031) to the FEC to replace departed Republican commissioners; a law-firm update says no confirmation hearing had been scheduled as of August 2026 and the FEC would regain a quorum only if both are confirmed.

In Bernegger v. FEC (D.D.C., No. 26-213), the FEC files a notice that it has two commissioners, has lacked a quorum since 2025-05-01 and cannot authorize the defense of the action; it notes two nominations announced on 2026-02-11 were still pending. An equivalent notice was filed in Seegers v. FEC on 2026-04-24 and does not mention DOJ.

Supreme Court decides NRSC v. FEC, 6-3 (Kavanaugh, J.), holding that FECA's limits on party spending coordinated with candidates violate the First Amendment; argued 2025-12-09, with the Solicitor General's office supporting the challengers and a court-appointed amicus defending the limits.

In Seegers v. FEC (D.D.C., No. 1:26-cv-00276), the clerk enters default against the FEC for failing to plead or defend; the plaintiff's default-judgment filings (dated 2026-07-28) report that the U.S. Attorney for D.C. was served 2026-02-24 and the Attorney General by certified mail delivered 2026-03-04, and describe no appearance or response by DOJ.
